user_turns:
Sunday night my boyfriend left his phone unlocked on the couch while he showered, and a text from his ex lit up the screen. I opened it. I'm not proud of that. But I scrolled back to February, and they've texted every single week since. Every week, for eight months at least. His ex wrote "Nobody gets me like you do" and Jun wrote back "Ha. Same." In August Jun told him talking to him is "the easiest part of my week." In June he ran to his ex about a fight we had about money, and the ex told him "You deserve easy."

When I asked Jun on Tuesday how often they talk, he said "now and then." Now and then! Then I told him what I'd seen, and he turned it around on me, about me looking at his phone. Turns out the ex's dad has dementia, which is a lot of what they text about, and Jun never once mentioned it to me. I think he kept it all quiet because he knew how it would look.

He's been sleeping in the spare room since Tuesday and I feel sick about all of it. How do I get him to talk about the ex without it turning into another fight about the phone?

results.result:
The phone and the ex aren't actually separable, and I don't think you should try to keep them separate. He's using the phone as a shield because it works — every time you bring up what you read, he gets to talk about how you read it. So the goal isn't to avoid the phone topic. It's to take it off the table so fast and so completely that he can't hide behind it anymore.

**Own the phone once, fully, with no "but."**

Something like: "I opened your phone and read eight months of your texts. That was a violation of your privacy and I'd be upset too if you did it to me. I'm not going to defend it." Then stop. Don't say "but I found..." in the same breath. Let it sit. If he keeps coming back to the phone after that, you can say, "I already told you I was wrong. I'm not going to keep re-apologizing so we can avoid the rest of this." Once you've genuinely conceded it, his returning to it starts looking like what it is — deflection.

**Lead with the lie, not the texts.**

The texts themselves are murky — he'll say it's about the dad, it's platonic, you're reading tone into it. "Now and then" isn't murky. You asked him a direct question and he gave you an answer he knew was false. That's the thing to ask about: *"When I asked how often you talk, why did you say 'now and then'?"* The honest answer to that is going to tell you a lot. If he knew weekly texts would look bad to you, he already knew something about this relationship wasn't fine.

**Then the questions you actually need answered:**

- Why did you never mention his dad has dementia? That's a sad, heavy thing happening to someone you care about — why was I the one person who couldn't know?
- Why did you take our money fight to him instead of back to me? And what did "you deserve easy" mean to you when you read it?
- What is this relationship to you? Not what is it technically — what is it actually?

Ask them as questions and let him answer. If he gives you a real answer, even an uncomfortable one, that's progress.

**Don't let the dementia erase what you read.**

The dad's illness is real and makes some of the texting make sense. It does not explain "Ha. Same" to "nobody gets me like you do," or "easiest part of my week," or going to him about your fight. Sympathetic context and emotional affair aren't mutually exclusive. You can hold both — "I understand you were supporting him through something awful" *and* "you built an emotional life with him that you hid from me."

**And be ready for it to go badly.**

He's been in the spare room four days. That's its own answer to something. If you make a clean apology about the phone and he still can't talk about the ex without turning it on you — that's not a communication problem you can fix with better phrasing. That's him telling you he'd rather lose the argument than have the conversation. You'd want to know that.

About the things that matter, yes. He lied to your face when you asked a direct question. He hid something emotionally significant for eight months. He took a fight with you to someone whose reply was essentially "you'd be happier without this." Those aren't interpretations — those are things that happened, and his explanation so far has been to change the subject. You're not crazy and you're not overreacting.

But I'd push back on the question a little, because "am I right" is the wrong frame for the conversation you're about to have.

You were also wrong about the phone, and that's not nothing — it's not nothing *to him*, and if you walk in holding a scorecard where your one wrong is dwarfed by his several wrongs, he'll feel that and dig in. People can tell when an apology is a toll you're paying to get to the accusation.

And "right" implies there's a verdict. There isn't. You don't actually know yet what the ex is to him. It might be an emotional affair he's half-aware of and ashamed of. It might be a friendship with his hand too far on the scale because the dad is dying and he didn't know how to tell you without it sounding like what it looks like. Those are different situations with different endings, and you can only find out which by asking questions you don't already know the answer to.

So: you're right that something is wrong, you're right that he lied, you're right to be sick about it. Go in with that, not with the verdict. The verdict is what you'll come out with.
